questions.question: In January 1610 Galileo pointed his telescope at a planet and found four moons going round it. Which planet?
questions.hint: He named the moons after the Medici, the ruling family of Florence. Today they are called Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.
questions.explanation: On 7 January 1610 Galileo saw three small "stars" beside Jupiter. Within a week he had found a fourth and understood that they were moons. He published the discovery in March in a short book, the Starry Messenger, and they are still called the Galilean moons.

questions.question: In which book, published in 1687, did Isaac Newton set out his three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation?
questions.hint: It is written in Latin, in three parts. The astronomer Edmond Halley pushed Newton to write it and paid for the printing himself.
questions.explanation: The full title is Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica, "Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy". It showed that the same force makes an apple fall and keeps the Moon in its orbit. Opticks is Newton's later book, of 1704.

image.alt: A portrait of a man with long grey hair, in a plain dark gown.

sources.label: Cambridge Digital Library, manuscript of Newton's Principia (Royal Society MS/69)

questions.question: In 1633 the Roman Inquisition put Galileo on trial and made him deny an idea that he had defended. Which idea?
options: That the Earth is a sphere
That the Earth moves round the Sun
That the universe has no end
That the orbits of the planets are ellipses
questions.hint: The idea came from the Polish astronomer Copernicus, whose book of 1543 the Church had suspended in 1616.
questions.explanation: On 22 June 1633 Galileo was found "vehemently suspected of heresy" and had to deny on his knees that the Earth moves. He spent his last years under house arrest in his villa at Arcetri, near Florence. There is no proof that he then muttered "And yet it moves".

image.alt: A painting: a man in dark red stands facing three churchmen at a table with a red cloth; a crucifix hangs on the wall.

questions.question: In the 1660s Newton passed a beam of sunlight through a glass prism in a dark room. What did his experiments show?
options: That light needs time to travel through space
That white light is a mix of colours
questions.hint: He then sent one part of the beam through a second prism, and it did not change again. He described what he saw with the Latin word "spectrum".
questions.explanation: Before Newton, people thought that white light was pure and simple, and that the prism changed it. He showed that white light already contains all the colours, and that the prism only separates them. He counted seven colours, perhaps to match the seven notes of the musical scale.

image.alt: A portrait of a man in a long curly wig and a loose robe over an open white shirt.

questions.question: Through his telescope Galileo saw that one planet shows phases like the Moon, from a thin crescent to a full disc. This fitted the system of Copernicus. Which planet?
questions.hint: Galileo watched it at the end of 1610. He first announced the discovery as a Latin anagram, a puzzle of mixed-up letters, so that nobody could steal it.
questions.explanation: A planet can show the full set of phases only if it goes round the Sun and not round the Earth. Galileo later gave the solution of his anagram: "The mother of loves imitates the shapes of Cynthia", which means that Venus copies the Moon.

image.alt: A portrait of a man of about forty with short hair and a beard; gold letters beside his head give his name in Latin.

questions.question: At which university did Galileo teach mathematics from 1592 to 1610, years that he later called the best of his life?
questions.hint: He built his first telescopes in that city. The university, founded in 1222, still shows a wooden teaching desk that, by tradition, his students built for him.
questions.explanation: Padua belonged to the Republic of Venice, which left its professors unusually free. In 1609 Galileo showed his telescope to the Venetian senators from the bell tower of St Mark's. In 1610 he left for Florence, to serve the Grand Duke of Tuscany.

image.alt: A wall painting: a man shows a long telescope to an old ruler in a gold robe and white fur, with other men watching by a window.

questions.question: In 1665 the University of Cambridge closed, and the young Newton went home to his family's farm, where he did some of his greatest work. Why had the university closed?
questions.hint: London suffered most that year, and Samuel Pepys described it in his famous diary.
questions.explanation: The Great Plague of 1665 killed perhaps 100,000 people in London. At Woolsthorpe, in Lincolnshire, Newton worked on gravity, on light and on the mathematics now called calculus. The story that a falling apple there set him thinking comes from Newton himself, late in his life.

questions.question: In 1696 Newton left Cambridge for London to help run a royal institution. He was its Master from 1699 until his death. Which institution?
questions.hint: He took the job seriously and hunted down counterfeiters in person. One of them, William Chaloner, was hanged in 1699.
questions.explanation: Newton became Warden of the Royal Mint in 1696 and Master in 1699. He helped to run the great recoinage, when the old silver coins of England were melted down and struck again. He was knighted in 1705 and is buried in Westminster Abbey.

questions.question: Which pope, once a friend and admirer of Galileo, was reigning when the Inquisition condemned him in 1633?
questions.hint: He was born Maffeo Barberini, in Florence. Bernini made the great bronze canopy over the altar of St Peter's for him.
questions.explanation: As a cardinal, Maffeo Barberini had written a Latin poem in praise of Galileo. But in the Dialogue of 1632 the pope's own argument is spoken by a character called Simplicio, and it seems that Urban felt mocked. In 1992 Pope John Paul II said that the theologians of Galileo's time had made an error.

questions.question: "If I have seen further, it is by standing on the shoulders of giants." To which scientist did Newton write these words in a letter?
questions.hint: He was in charge of experiments at the Royal Society, and his book Micrographia has the first drawing of cells seen under a microscope. He and Newton became bitter enemies.
questions.explanation: Newton wrote the sentence to Robert Hooke in February 1676, during a polite pause in their quarrel about light. Later Hooke said that Newton had taken the idea of the law of gravity from him. The image of dwarfs on the shoulders of giants was already old: it goes back to Bernard of Chartres in the twelfth century.
